cases.learnTitle: Lung cancer (adenocarcinoma) on chest CT (radiologists' box)
cases.contextSource: Collection description (Lung-PET-CT-Dx: patients with biopsy-confirmed lung cancer; histology from the patient ID).
cases.referenceSummary: The tumor is boxed on every slice where the dataset's thoracic radiologists marked it (9 boxes on 9 images of this series (display positions 34-42 of 51)). Histology: adenocarcinoma. Nodes, metastases and other findings are not marked.
cases.learnNotes: Bronchogenic carcinoma shows itself in several ways: a solitary nodule or mass (often with spiculated or lobulated margins), a central mass with collapse of the lung beyond an obstructed bronchus, hilar or mediastinal enlargement from nodes, or direct invasion of the chest wall, mediastinum or vertebrae. On CT read the lungs on a lung window and the mediastinum on a soft-tissue window; describe the size, the lobe, the margins, contact with the pleura, fissures and vessels, and look for nodes, effusion and bone lesions. Imaging cannot tell the cell type; the biopsy does.

cases.learnTitle: Hepatocellular carcinoma on contrast CT (tumor and liver segmented)
cases.clinicalContext: Adult referred for a multiphase liver CT.
cases.contextSource: Collection description (HCC-TACE-Seg: confirmed HCC, baseline CT before the first TACE).
cases.referenceSummary: The tumor, the liver and the abdominal aorta were segmented semi-automatically and clinically curated (HCC-TACE-Seg). Only the contrast phase the segmentation was drawn on is installed, so the washout on later phases cannot be shown here.
cases.learnNotes: Hepatocellular carcinoma usually arises in a cirrhotic liver. On multiphase CT its typical behavior is arterial-phase hyperenhancement (brighter than the liver) with washout on later phases (darker than the liver), often with an enhancing capsule. Large tumors are heterogeneous and may invade the portal or hepatic veins. Compare every phase; a metastasis is usually darker than the liver on the portal venous phase, and a hemangioma fills in from the periphery.

cases.learnTitle: Vestibular schwannoma on contrast T1 and high-resolution T2 (manual contour)
cases.contextSource: Collection description (Vestibular-Schwannoma-SEG: patients treated with Gamma Knife radiosurgery).
cases.referenceSummary: The tumor was contoured manually on every axial slice by the treating neurosurgeon and physicist, on both sequences (Gamma Knife planning). The cochlea and planning structures are not shown.
cases.learnNotes: A vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) arises from the vestibular nerve in the internal auditory canal and grows into the cerebellopontine angle. It is extra-axial: CSF clefts and vessels separate it from the brainstem and cerebellum. On contrast T1 it enhances strongly, often like an ice-cream cone with the cone in the internal auditory canal; on high-resolution T2 it is a dark filling defect in the bright CSF. The main alternative at the cerebellopontine angle is a meningioma, which is broad-based on the dura, may have a dural tail and rarely enters the canal.

tasks.explanation: A vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) arises from the vestibular nerve in the internal auditory canal and grows into the cerebellopontine angle. It is extra-axial: CSF clefts and vessels separate it from the brainstem and cerebellum. On contrast T1 it enhances strongly, often like an ice-cream cone with the cone in the internal auditory canal; on high-resolution T2 it is a dark filling defect in the bright CSF. The main alternative at the cerebellopontine angle is a meningioma, which is broad-based on the dura, may have a dural tail and rarely enters the canal.

tasks.title: Inside or outside the brain?
tasks.prompt: Is the posterior fossa mass intra-axial (arising within the brain substance) or extra-axial (arising outside the brain, from the coverings, nerves or spaces around it)?

options.why: It sits in the cerebellopontine angle cistern, separated from the brainstem and cerebellum by CSF, and extends into the internal auditory canal.
An intra-axial mass would be surrounded by brain tissue and expand it from within; here CSF separates the mass from the brain.

hints.text: On the T2 series look for bright CSF between the mass and the brainstem or cerebellum.

tasks.explanation: Extra-axial masses displace the brain and are separated from it by CSF clefts and vessels; the commonest at the cerebellopontine angle are vestibular schwannoma and meningioma.
